newsitem.title: USA: Wheat price rebound may ease U.S.-Europe tension.
newsitem.headline: Wheat price rebound may ease U.S.-Europe tension.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman forecast higher wheat prices Wednesday, a development that might reduce the chances of a new export subsidy war between Europe and the United States.

Glickman was to meet Franz Fischler, his European Union counterpart, over dinner Thursday in Rome with export subsidies one of the topics for discussion. Genetically engineered foods, another sensitive issue, also were on the agenda.
U.S. officials have closely monitored the EU's resumption of subsidised wheat exports this fall and the rising size of the subsidies. There have been calls for U.S. retaliation.
During a telephone news conference from Rome, Glickman told reporters that wheat prices appeared too low in light of the comparatively tight supply.
"Given that, I think you're going to see higher prices come back," Glickman said. "I think what you're going to see is some upward pressure on the markets. I think it's already begun to happen."

Earlier in the day, an EU official said budget pressures would constrain use of European export subsidies. Congress has limited the major U.S. export subsidy programme to $100 million this fiscal year, one-tenth of previous levels.

Analysts said higher wheat prices would ease the pressure for either side to subsidise wheat exports. While the European Union reaped a bumper crop of nearly 98 million metric tons and wants to export a third of it, the U.S. crop was 2.3 billion bushels, or 62 million tons.

"We don't have a case now" for U.S. export subsidies, said private consultant John Schnittker, but he warned the situation could change if the EU awarded lavish discounts in the face of a rising market.
Two other consultants said U.S. wheat prices were still at high levels despite falling from stratospheric mid-summer marks when world stockpiles were small.
"I think there will be a lot of talk about low wheat prices," said analyst Bill Lesher, but "not a lot will come of it," including demands for export subsidies.
The other analyst, who asked not to be named, said use of export subsidies was "a political question" and "an emotional thing."

During the telephone news conference, Glickman said China's threat of a temporary ban on imports of some U.S. farm goods was a cause of concern but he had no list of specific targets. He also said a dispute with Turkey over wheat import standards appeared on the way to being resolved.
